headline: Hormuz Traffic Falls to a Trickle
deck: CENTCOM says the strait remains open under military support while its Iran-port blockade redirects and disables vessels. Houthi attacks have added pressure at the Red Sea’s southern gate.
body: U.S. Central Command completed a thirteenth consecutive night of strikes against Iranian targets on 23 July. [E1] It named command centres, drone storage, communications, coastal surveillance and maritime capabilities among the targets. [E1] CENTCOM said the campaign was intended to reduce threats to civilian mariners and commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. [E1] The same statement said the waterway remained open with U.S. military support.

Open has become a thin word. Public shipping data cited on 24 July counted six vessels through Hormuz, a trickle compared with ordinary traffic. [E3] Some ships used the northern route preferred by Iran, while the U.S. blockade continued around Iranian ports. [E2][E3] A legal channel can remain available while commercial operators decide that the voyage is too exposed.

Blockade enforcement is now visible in hulls. CENTCOM said it had redirected 12 commercial vessels, disabled two that did not comply and boarded two for verification by 25 July. [E2] The Mozambique-flagged tanker Lavine was disabled after repeated warnings, while the Comoros-flagged Charminar continued after a boarding. [E2] Those outcomes show a selective system: port destination and compliance decide which cargo advances.

Pressure has also moved toward Bab el-Mandeb. Public reporting described increased traffic through the Red Sea gate as Hormuz volumes fell, even as the Houthis claimed strikes on Saudi energy sites and Saudi forces answered in Yemen. [E3] A route chosen to escape one danger can inherit another. Tankers do not need both straits to close before owners add distance, delay and risk to the barrel.

The observable ledger is smaller than the rhetoric. No public source establishes a complete physical closure of Hormuz, and commercial vessels still pass. [E1][E3] CENTCOM’s count measures its own interventions rather than every transit, while daily public tallies can change with weather, scheduling and reporting lag. The evidence supports severe friction and selective interdiction.

Adaptation supplies the strongest null. Escorts, compliant boardings, northern passages and longer routes can keep enough oil moving to prevent a durable dual-chokepoint shock. [E1][E2][E3] Mediation can also lower the risk premium before normal traffic returns. Six ships are evidence of a market under pressure, not proof that the next seven days will look the same.

Oil traders are pricing a route with two armed tollbooths and several imperfect exits. The U.S. says Hormuz is open, Iran asserts control over southern passages, and Houthi fire keeps the alternative corridor unsettled. [E1][E2][E3] The barrel has not disappeared. It has acquired more people who can stop it.
